belief: My boss will always find fault with me.
origins: A critical parent, teacher, or earlier boss can train us to scan every authority figure for disapproval. At work, a brief tone or a correction can feel like proof that we are in trouble. If we have actually worked under harsh managers, we may expect it everywhere.
teaches: Paul says, “Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men,” and “Serve with good will, as to the Lord and not to men, because you know that the Lord will reward each one for whatever good he does.” Our final evaluator is not our manager. Proverbs says, “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” And “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone.” We take feedback seriously without letting criticism define us. Some bosses are unfair, and then boundaries, documentation, and wise counsel may be needed.
self_statements: No matter what I do, they will criticize me.
Every email from my boss is a warning.
I am always one mistake from trouble.
They have it in for me.
errors: Treating one correction as constant fault-finding.
Focusing on criticism and missing positive feedback.
Taking neutral comments as personal attacks.
questions: What has my boss actually said or done, as opposed to what I assume?
Have I received any praise or neutral feedback that I discounted?
Whom did I first expect to find fault with me?
Is the feedback accurate, and what can I learn from it?
If the boss really is unfair, what steps are wise?
Whom do I ultimately work for?
truth: I can work wholeheartedly for the Lord and receive feedback without being crushed by it. I can distinguish fair critique from my fear. If the treatment really is unfair, I can respond with wisdom, boundaries, and help.
hw_truths: I work for the Lord first.
Feedback is information, not a verdict.
A gentle answer turns away wrath.
God knows I am dust and has compassion.
I am not defined by my boss’s opinion.
log: Each day, write one factual piece of feedback and one thing that went well.
actions: Write down actual comments from your boss for two weeks.
Request a short meeting about expectations.
Respond calmly, “Thank you, I will work on that.”
If treatment seems unfair, talk to HR or a wise adviser.
prayer: Lord, I work for You first. Calm my fear of criticism, help me learn from fair feedback, and give me wisdom when treatment is unfair. Amen.
hw_questions: What has my boss actually said?
What positive feedback have I received?
Whom do I expect to criticize me?
name_example: Sarah can write: “I work for the Lord first, so my boss’s opinion does not define me.”
meta: Christian belief counseling for “My boss will always find fault with me.” with BSB scriptures, questions, songs, and practical homework.
